  • 💬 Discord — join the frontend best-practices community: discord.gg/d9KRhuAwQ
  • 📸 Instagram — frontend best practices, daily: @bestpractice___

articles.title: The Junior Developer Comeback: Seniors will struggle to get a job?
articles.description: Right now, juniors are struggling.  Whether you're trying to become a developer, a designer, or a...
articles.body_html:
Right now, juniors are struggling.

Whether you're trying to become a developer, a designer, or a data analyst, the entry-level door feels like it's closing. Seniors, on the other hand, are mostly getting hired or retained.

I think that's about to reverse. Not this year, but within the next five to ten years, I believe juniors will do very well, and seniors will be the ones fighting for jobs.

Let me explain.

Learn Git by completing missions

Why juniors are struggling right now

The current state of AI is good, but it isn't senior-level good.

It can write code, generate designs, and crunch data. But it still needs someone experienced to guide it, catch its mistakes, and make the calls that actually matter. That's exactly what a senior does.

So companies are doing the logical thing for today's reality:

  • Keep the seniors, because they can steer AI and fix what it gets wrong.
  • Skip the juniors, because AI already covers a lot of what juniors used to do.

That's the world we're in right now, and it explains why the junior market feels so rough.

What happens in 5 to 10 years?

Now fast forward.

By then, AI will probably be senior-level good. Not "impressive for a tool," but genuinely capable of senior-level work.

Here's the part that matters: someone still has to operate it.

Even with extremely capable AI, people will need some technical skill to use it well. Not a lot, but some. You need enough understanding to describe what you want, to judge whether the output is right, and to know when something is off.

And not everyone will have that.

Most people won't have spent time learning graphic design, web development, or data analysis. The people who did will have a real edge, because they understand the fundamentals well enough to operate the AI properly.

The incentive to hire seniors disappears

This is where the economics flip.

Picture two candidates:

Senior Junior (with some technical skill)
Output with senior-level AI Great Just as great
Salary expectation High Much lower

If AI closes the gap in raw capability, then the senior's main advantage, years of hard-won technical expertise, matters a lot less. The junior with a bit of technical knowledge gets the same job done just as well.

The senior costs more and delivers about the same result.

From a business perspective, the decision becomes easy. Why pay more for a result you can get for less? The incentive to hire a senior drops, and hiring a junior with some technical knowledge starts to make far more sense.

Where I could be wrong

I don't want to pretend this is a certainty. A few things could change the picture:

  • Seniors might shift their value. If the gap in technical execution disappears, seniors could compete on things AI doesn't replace, like judgment, product sense, communication, and owning the consequences when something breaks.
  • "A little technical skill" might not be enough. If AI makes mistakes that are subtle or expensive, companies may still pay for deep expertise as insurance.
  • Timelines are uncertain. Five to ten years is a guess, and AI progress has surprised people in both directions.
  • The pipeline problem. If nobody hires juniors for years, fewer people will build the technical foundation that this whole argument depends on.

Even so, I think the core pressure is real: when capability gets cheap, the premium for experience shrinks.

What this means for you

If you're a junior: Don't give up on learning the fundamentals. The market is hard right now, but the technical foundation you build is the thing that could set you apart later. Learn the craft, and learn to work with AI, not against it.

If you're a senior: Don't rely on years of experience alone. Lean into what's hardest to automate, such as decision-making, system thinking, and being the person who can be trusted with outcomes, not just output.

Final thoughts

Today's market rewards seniors because AI isn't senior-level yet. Tomorrow's market might reward cheaper people who can operate a senior-level AI.

The people who win won't necessarily be the most experienced. They'll be the ones who have just enough technical skill to get the most out of the tools.

I could be completely off, so I'd love to hear what you think.

Do you think juniors will bounce back once AI reaches senior-level ability, or will seniors always have the upper hand? Let me know in the comments. 👇

articles.title: The Most Precise Plugin in My Benchmark Scored 10.8%
articles.description: Six ESLint security plugins, one labelled corpus, same harness, same day — F1 from 10.5% to 100%. I wrote the corpus, which is the most important sentence in the article and changes how every row should be read.
articles.body_html:
Six ESLint security plugins, one labelled corpus of 69 vulnerable fixtures,
same harness, same day — eslint-plugin-security@4.0.1,
@microsoft/eslint-plugin-sdl@1.1.0, ESLint 10.8.1, Node 24.

I wrote the fixtures. That sentence has to come before the table, because
it changes what every row below is worth.

TP, FP and FN are
the four boxes everything below is derived from.

Plugin TP FP FN F1
Interlace 69 0 0 100%
eslint-plugin-sonarjs 27 9 42 51.4%
eslint-plugin-security 10 7 59 23.3%
@microsoft/eslint-plugin-sdl 6 2 63 15.6%
eslint-plugin-no-unsanitized 4 1 65 10.8%
eslint-plugin-security-node 4 3 65 10.5%

Three rows have a piece of their own, linked above — one tool read closely
rather than ranked. This is seventeen plugins
compressed into one table, and compression is the subject.

Read the column the ranking hides

F1 blends precision and recall, which is how a table like this stops being
informative. Split them and a different tool leads.

eslint-plugin-no-unsanitized sits second from the bottom at 10.8% F1. Its
precision is 80% — 4 true positives against 1 false positive, the highest
of any community plugin here. It detects four things. It is right about
substantially all of them.

That is not a consolation prize. A tool with 80% precision and a narrow scope
is one you leave switched on. A tool that finds more and is wrong more often is
one somebody disables in month three — and a rule nobody runs has a recall of
zero regardless of what the table says.

Why my row says 100%, and why you should discount it

A 100% row against fixtures written by the people who wrote the rules is the
expected outcome of grading your own homework. It is not evidence of
superiority and I will not present it as any.

What it is: a regression gate we happen to publish. It says our rules still
detect what we built them to detect. On the day it stops saying 100%, something
broke.

Three limits follow:

  • The fixtures encode our threat model. A plugin scoped to a different surface — browser DOM, Angular, Electron — scores low here for reasons that say nothing about its quality on that surface.
  • F1 on a self-authored corpus measures agreement with our idea of the problem, not correctness in the world.
  • Recall against 69 of my fixtures is not recall against the field.

@microsoft/eslint-plugin-sdl is the clean example: 15.6% here, and it is a
well-made tool aimed at frontend and Microsoft-stack hardening. Pointing a
Node-backend corpus at it measures the mismatch, not the plugin.

The check I ran before publishing any of it

I did not take the F1 column on trust — including my own row.

Every value was recomputed from its own TP/FP/FN with 2·P·R/(P+R). All six
matched the published figure to within a tenth of a point. Then the check that
actually matters: TP + FN = 69 on every row. If those totals disagreed, the
rows would be describing six differently-scoped runs and the table would not be
a comparison at all.

A minute's work, and the difference between a table you can defend and one you
copied. A number without its measurement is a memory,
and a rank throws away the distribution behind it — a leaderboard is
the least recoverable form a measurement can take.

What the table is for

Not for picking a plugin. For two narrower things.

A scope map. The recall column tells you what each tool was built to see.
Four of 69 is not failure; it is a statement of scope, useful when you are
deciding what to run alongside what.

A regression gate. Which is what it is to me, and the only claim here I
would defend without qualification.

If you want the version of this you can trust without knowing me, run it
yourself. The corpus and the harness are in
the plugins repo under
benchmarks/, and the suite that produced this table is one command:

npx tsx benchmarks/suites/ilb-juliet/run.ts

Pin the versions above or your numbers will not match mine — eslint-plugin-security's
recall moves between releases, which is exactly why an unpinned comparison
table is worth nothing. Then add fixtures for the threats you care about. The
result will disagree with mine, and yours will be the one worth having.

Whose fixtures is your security tooling being graded on — and have you ever read them?

articles.title: I built an open-source AI interface builder that exports to React, Vue, Svelte… and Roblox
articles.description: Drag components onto a canvas, ask any AI model to build pages, and export to HTML, React, Vue, Svelte, Roblox Luau or LÖVE. Free and MIT-licensed.
articles.body_html:
Hey DEV 👋

I've been building openconstructor: a browser-based interface builder where you put together pages from ready-made blocks and an AI assistant. It's free, needs no install, and the whole thing is open source under MIT.

👉 Try it: https://openconstructor.pw
👉 Source: https://github.com/Kuloka/openconstructor

What it does

1. A real component library. There are 145 components in 12 sections: AI & Chat (chat windows, prompt composers, "thinking" indicators, agent steps), Dashboards and charts, Pricing & Commerce, Auth, Navigation, Landing sections, Effects and more. Each one is plain HTML + CSS with no framework lock-in. Animated components play when you hover them in the catalog. Browse the sections →

2. Bring your own AI. Connect a key from OpenRouter, Google Gemini, Groq, Cerebras, Mistral, DeepSeek, OpenAI, Anthropic, xAI or Together, then type "a pricing section with three plans". The block lands on the canvas. Select an element first and only that element gets changed.
Your keys stay in your browser and are sent only to the provider you picked. On a budget? Groq's no-cost plan with GPT-OSS 120B and Gemini Flash both work well. More on the AI generator →

3. Screenshot → blocks. Paste a screenshot of any site or mockup (Ctrl+V works) and a vision model rebuilds it as editable HTML/CSS.

4. Edit without code. Double-click an element to edit its text directly on the page. Click any part of it to change color, size, weight, radius or padding in a small inspector.

5. ⚗ Fusion. This is the experiment I'm most curious about. Right-click a component → fuse with… → click another one. The AI breeds a new component that does the first one's job in the second one's visual style. A sign-in form × a glassmorphism card gives you a glass sign-in form, in its own new design rather than a copy of either.

6. Responsive by default (if you want). Switch the page from free layout to stack. Blocks then flow top to bottom, and the export adapts to any screen. A preview shows the page on phone, tablet and desktop side by side.

7. Page-wide themes. One click recolors every component on the page to a new accent. Grays stay gray, and alpha and notation are preserved. You can also swap any single color everywhere, or set one font and one corner style for the whole page.

Export anywhere, including game engines

This is the part I haven't seen in other web builders:

  • HTML: one self-contained file
  • React / Vue / Svelte: a ready component file
  • Roblox (Luau): a LocalScript that builds your UI with ScreenGui, Frame, TextLabel, TextButton, UICorner, UIStroke, UIGradient and a UIScale that fits any screen. Drop it into StarterPlayerScripts and press Play. How it works →
  • LÖVE 2D (Lua): a main.lua that draws the layout with love.graphics. Details →
  • Flutter, SwiftUI, Jetpack Compose, Tailwind: AI-assisted ports, a starting point to review.

The Roblox and LÖVE exports don't guess from your HTML. They read the rendered layout, using each element's real position, size, colors, radius, borders and text, and then generate native UI code from that snapshot. To be clear, they're visual only: buttons and text boxes have no logic wired up yet.

Share it

Hit publish and the page gets a public link like openconstructor.pw/p/my-page. Signed-in users can also keep projects in the cloud and open them on any device. Sign-in is optional, and everything else works without an account.

How it's built

  • Vite + vanilla JS for the editor. React 19 only for the landing page and the chat input.
  • Every element renders in its own sandboxed iframe with a strict CSP and no scripts. AI-generated code can't touch the editor or your keys.
  • Supabase for auth (Google, GitHub, email) and storage.
  • Cloudflare for hosting. A small Worker serves published pages, sandboxed with script-src 'none'.

What's next

I'd love feedback, especially on:

  • Which export target you'd actually use, and what's missing from it
  • Components you wish were in the library
  • Whether Fusion produces anything useful for you, or just chaos 😄

Issues and PRs are very welcome: https://github.com/Kuloka/openconstructor

If you like the project, a ⭐ on GitHub really helps a solo dev get it in front of more people. Thanks for reading!

articles.title: Angular Monorepos: When Does It Actually Make Sense?
articles.description: Angular applications rarely stay small forever.  A project starts with a single application, a few...
articles.body_html:
Angular applications rarely stay small forever.

A project starts with a single application, a few components, and some services. Over time, new requirements appear. Another application is introduced. Teams start sharing components, models, and utilities.

Eventually, someone suggests:

"We should move everything into a monorepo and use Nx."

And honestly, that might be a good idea.

But is it always necessary?

Angular CLI already supports multiple projects in a workspace. Nx adds powerful capabilities for dependency management, task execution, caching, and CI optimization, but those capabilities come with additional concepts and tooling.

So, when does Nx actually make sense?

Rather than simply explaining what a monorepo is, I want to explore this through a practical example, compare Angular CLI with Nx, and understand what changes when a workspace grows.

The goal isn't to prove that Nx is better.

The goal is to understand when the benefits of Nx justify its additional complexity.

1. First, What Problem Are We Trying to Solve?

Let's imagine a company with two Angular applications:

  • An administrative dashboard.
  • A customer portal.

Both applications display information about vehicles, appointments, and operational status.

Initially, they are completely independent.

company/
├── admin-app/
└── customer-app/

Each application has its own dependencies, configuration, and deployment pipeline.

This is a perfectly reasonable architecture.

However, the applications eventually start sharing code:

  • UI components.
  • Domain models.
  • API clients.
  • Validation utilities.
  • Design system elements.

Now we have a few options:

  1. Duplicate the code.
  2. Create an internal npm package.
  3. Share code through a monorepo.
  4. Introduce a workspace tool such as Nx.

The important distinction is that sharing code and sharing a repository are two different decisions.

A shared npm package can work perfectly well across separate repositories. A monorepo becomes particularly interesting when applications need to coordinate their dependencies, development, testing, and releases.

Before introducing a new tool, we should understand which problem we are actually solving.

2. Angular CLI Already Supports Monorepos

This is something that is sometimes overlooked.

Angular CLI is not limited to a single application per repository.

It supports workspaces containing multiple applications and libraries.

Let's create one.

Creating an Angular workspace 

ng new company-platform --no-create-application

cd company-platform

Now we can generate multiple applications:

ng generate application admin

ng generate application customer

And shared libraries:

ng generate library shared-ui

ng generate library shared-data

Our workspace now looks something like this:

company-platform/
├── projects/
│   ├── admin/
│   ├── customer/
│   ├── shared-ui/
│   └── shared-data/
├── angular.json
├── package.json
├── tsconfig.json
└── node_modules/

The exact generated files depend on the Angular version and project configuration, but the overall structure is familiar.

Angular CLI provides commands for building, testing, serving, and generating code across these projects.

For example:

ng serve admin

ng build customer

ng test admin

We can also build libraries:

ng build shared-ui

For many workspaces, this is already enough.

Sharing a component

Let's create a reusable vehicle card.

// projects/shared-ui/src/lib/vehicle-card/vehicle-card.component.ts

import { Component, input } from '@angular/core';

export interface Vehicle {
  id: string;
  registration: string;
  model: string;
}

@Component({
  selector: 'shared-vehicle-card',
  standalone: true,
  template: `
    <article>
      <h3>{{ vehicle().registration }}</h3>
      <p>{{ vehicle().model }}</p>
    </article>
  `,
})
export class VehicleCardComponent {
  vehicle = input.required<Vehicle>();
}

We can export it from the library's public API:

// projects/shared-ui/src/public-api.ts

export * from './lib/vehicle-card/vehicle-card.component';

Then the admin application can import it:

import { Component } from '@angular/core';

import { VehicleCardComponent } from 'shared-ui';

@Component({
  selector: 'app-vehicle-list',
  standalone: true,
  imports: [VehicleCardComponent],
  template: `
    @for (vehicle of vehicles; track vehicle.id) {
      <shared-vehicle-card [vehicle]="vehicle" />
    }
  `,
})
export class VehicleListComponent {
  vehicles: Vehicle[] = [];
}

The customer application can use the same library.

This is a legitimate monorepo setup.

And we haven't needed Nx yet.

If your main requirement is simply sharing Angular libraries between a few applications, Angular CLI might already solve your problem.

3. What Changes When We Introduce Nx?

Nx doesn't replace Angular.

It builds on the Angular ecosystem and adds capabilities for managing larger workspaces.

According to the official Nx comparison, Angular CLI already supports application generation, libraries, building, testing, and local development.

Nx adds capabilities such as:

  • First-class monorepo tooling.
  • Project dependency graphs.
  • Enforced module boundaries.
  • Affected task execution.
  • Task orchestration.
  • Local task caching.
  • Remote caching.
  • Distributed task execution.

These are the differences worth exploring.

Creating an Nx workspace

We can create a new Angular workspace with Nx:

npx create-nx-workspace@latest company-platform \
  --template=nrwl/angular-template

The Angular template is available through Nx's workspace creation workflow.

Alternatively, we can migrate an existing Angular CLI workspace incrementally.

From the existing workspace:

npx nx add @nx/angular

This installs the Angular plugin and configures Nx integration.

It's important to keep Nx package versions compatible with each other. Using nx add is the recommended way to install the plugin into an existing Nx workspace.

Documentation:

  • Nx with Angular
  • Adding Nx to an existing workspace

Generating applications and libraries

With Nx, we can generate applications:

nx generate @nx/angular:app apps/admin

nx generate @nx/angular:app apps/customer

And libraries:

nx generate @nx/angular:lib libs/shared-ui

nx generate @nx/angular:lib libs/shared-data

Nx also supports more specific libraries:

nx generate @nx/angular:lib libs/vehicles/feature-list

nx generate @nx/angular:lib libs/vehicles/data-access

nx generate @nx/angular:lib libs/vehicles/ui

The exact generator options depend on the Nx and Angular versions, so check the Angular generator reference when building a real workspace.

A possible structure:

company-platform/
├── apps/
│   ├── admin/
│   └── customer/
│
├── libs/
│   ├── shared/
│   │   ├── ui/
│   │   └── data-access/
│   │
│   └── vehicles/
│       ├── feature-list/
│       ├── data-access/
│       └── ui/
│
├── nx.json
├── package.json
└── tsconfig.base.json

This organization makes it easier to understand which libraries belong to which domain.

However, the folder structure alone isn't the most important difference.

The real value starts when Nx understands the relationships between projects.

4. Project Graph: Understanding Dependencies

Imagine our workspace has these projects:

admin
customer
shared-ui
vehicles-data-access
billing
reports

The applications depend on shared libraries:

admin
 ├── shared-ui
 └── vehicles-data-access

customer
 ├── shared-ui
 └── vehicles-data-access

As the workspace grows, these relationships become increasingly important.

A change to shared-ui might affect both applications.

A change to billing might affect only the administrative application.

Without a clear understanding of these dependencies, it's easy to lose track of what needs to be tested or rebuilt.

Nx builds a project graph that represents relationships between projects.

You can inspect it with:

nx graph

The interactive graph helps developers understand how applications and libraries depend on each other.

This becomes especially useful when a workspace contains dozens or hundreds of projects.

Angular CLI can manage multiple projects, but it doesn't provide the same first-class project graph visualization and dependency-aware workflow as Nx.

The distinction isn't that Angular CLI cannot organize projects.

It's that Nx makes relationships between projects a central part of the development workflow.

5. Enforcing Architectural Boundaries

This is one of the most interesting features of Nx.

Let's say we have two applications:

apps/
├── admin/
└── customer/

And some shared libraries:

libs/
├── shared/
│   ├── ui/
│   └── utils/
│
└── vehicles/
    ├── feature-list/
    └── data-access/

A reasonable dependency structure might be:

admin → vehicles/feature-list
admin → shared/ui

customer → vehicles/feature-list
customer → shared/ui

vehicles/feature-list → vehicles/data-access

vehicles/data-access → shared/utils

But what happens when someone starts importing application-specific code into a shared library?

For example:

// libs/shared/ui/src/lib/admin-widget.ts

import { AdminService } from
  '../../../../apps/admin/src/app/services/admin.service';

This is a serious architectural problem.

A shared library should not depend on a specific application.

The problem isn't merely that the import path is ugly.

The dependency direction is wrong.

The shared library now depends on an application that depends on the shared library.

This can create circular dependencies, difficult refactoring, and unpredictable build relationships.

Nx module boundary rules

Nx provides the @nx/enforce-module-boundaries ESLint rule.

We can use project tags to describe architectural roles.

For example:

{
  "name": "admin",
  "tags": ["scope:admin", "type:app"]
}

A shared UI library:

{
  "name": "shared-ui",
  "tags": ["scope:shared", "type:ui"]
}

A vehicles data-access library:

{
  "name": "vehicles-data-access",
  "tags": ["scope:vehicles", "type:data-access"]
}

We can then define dependency constraints in ESLint.

A simplified configuration might look like this:

// eslint.config.mjs

import nx from '@nx/eslint-plugin';

export default [
  {
    files: ['**/*.ts'],
    rules: {
      '@nx/enforce-module-boundaries': [
        'error',
        {
          depConstraints: [
            {
              sourceTag: 'type:app',
              onlyDependOnLibsWithTags: [
                'type:app',
                'type:feature',
                'type:ui',
                'type:data-access',
                'type:util',
              ],
            },
          ],
        },
      ],
    },
  },
];

This is an illustrative rule. A real workspace should define its constraints according to its architecture, and the exact ESLint configuration may vary with the Nx version and generated setup.

The important point is that Nx can help enforce architectural decisions instead of relying exclusively on code review.

This is a concrete benefit: Nx can help prevent certain dependency relationships from being introduced in the first place.

Angular CLI doesn't provide an equivalent first-class module-boundary enforcement feature.

6. The Performance Question: Is Nx Actually Faster?

This is where I think we need to be careful.

It's easy to find claims that Nx makes builds dramatically faster.

But performance depends on many factors:

  • Number of projects.
  • Number of dependencies.
  • Build configuration.
  • Test configuration.
  • Hardware.
  • CI environment.
  • Cache availability.
  • How much of the workspace changes.

A small Angular application might not see a meaningful improvement.

A large monorepo with many independent projects could benefit significantly.

Let's break down the relevant features.

6.1 Angular CLI already has caching

Before comparing Nx, we need to acknowledge something important.

Angular CLI already supports persistent disk caching.

For example:

ng build admin

Running the same build again can reuse cached work.

The cache is enabled by default for local development environments.

You can inspect its configuration:

ng cache info

And control it through the workspace configuration.

For example:

ng config cli.cache.environment all

Angular CLI cache documentation:

https://angular.dev/cli/cache

Therefore, it would be misleading to compare:

  • Angular CLI with caching disabled.
  • Nx with caching enabled.

That wouldn't be a fair comparison.

6.2 Nx adds task-level caching

Nx introduces caching at the task level.

A task might be:

nx build admin

Nx calculates a hash based on relevant inputs, including source files, dependencies, configuration, and other task inputs.

If the same task with the same relevant inputs has already completed, Nx can restore its cached outputs instead of executing the task again.

For example:

nx build admin

Run it again:

nx build admin

If the task is cacheable and its inputs haven't changed, Nx can restore the previous result.

This isn't simply caching Angular's compilation.

Nx can cache the results of different kinds of tasks, including builds, tests, linting, and other configured commands.

Documentation:

https://nx.dev/docs/features/cache-task-results

6.3 Running only affected projects

This is where Nx becomes particularly interesting.

Imagine a workspace with:

admin
customer
shared-ui
vehicles-data-access
billing
reports

A change to vehicles-data-access might affect:

vehicles-data-access
admin
customer

But it shouldn't necessarily require rebuilding:

billing
reports

Nx can determine which projects are affected by a change.

For example:

nx affected -t build

And:

nx affected -t test

These commands run the relevant tasks for affected projects.

This is particularly useful in CI, where running every build and test on every commit can become expensive.

The actual benefit depends on the dependency graph.

If every application depends on the same library, changing that library may affect nearly the entire workspace.

In that case, the number of skipped tasks will be smaller.

6.4 Parallel task execution

Nx can also run independent tasks in parallel.

For example:

nx run-many -t build

This runs build tasks across projects.

Nx's task graph determines which tasks can run concurrently and which depend on other tasks.

This can reduce total execution time when the workspace contains independent projects.

However, parallel execution also depends on available CPU and memory resources.

Running too many builds simultaneously can increase memory pressure and make the machine slower.

Parallelism is not automatically a performance improvement in every environment.

7. Remote Caching: A Different Kind of Benefit

Local caching is useful for individual developers.

Remote caching becomes particularly interesting for teams.

Imagine five developers working on the same workspace.

Developer A builds and tests a shared library.

Developer B later makes a change to an application that uses that library.

If the library's task inputs haven't changed, the previous result may be reusable.

Nx Cloud can share cache results between developers and CI environments.

This means the same task doesn't necessarily need to run repeatedly on every machine.

The workflow can look like this:

Developer A
    |
    | Build shared library
    v
Remote Cache
    |
    | Reuse result
    v
Developer B / CI

Nx Cloud documentation:

https://nx.dev/docs/features/ci-features/remote-cache

This can be valuable when:

  • Builds are expensive.
  • Many developers share the same workspace.
  • CI repeatedly executes similar tasks.
  • Projects have stable dependencies.

But remote caching introduces additional considerations:

  • Configuration.
  • Cache access and permissions.
  • Infrastructure or subscription costs, depending on the setup.
  • Correct task input and output configuration.

A cache is only useful when the system can safely determine that the previous result is valid.

8. Angular CLI vs Nx: A Practical Comparison

Let's summarize what we've discussed.

Capability Angular CLI Nx
Multiple Angular projects Yes Yes
Angular applications Yes Yes
Angular libraries Yes Yes
Shared components Yes Yes
Build, test, serve Yes Yes
Project dependency graph Limited compared with Nx First-class
Enforced module boundaries No equivalent built-in feature Yes
Affected project execution No equivalent first-class workflow Yes
Task-level caching Angular build cache Nx task cache
Remote caching Not built in Available through Nx Cloud
Distributed task execution Not built in Available through Nx Cloud
Additional tooling complexity Lower Higher

One detail matters here: Angular CLI and Nx are not mutually exclusive.

Nx integrates with Angular CLI builders and schematics.

You can continue using familiar Angular tooling while gradually introducing Nx features.

The official Nx comparison provides a more detailed overview.

9. Performance Benchmarks: Let's Measure Instead of Guessing

I think this is an important section to include in any serious comparison.

Rather than claiming that Nx is a certain percentage faster, we can create a reproducible benchmark.

Benchmark environment

Use a workspace with:

  • Two Angular applications.
  • Five shared libraries.
  • Unit tests for each application and library.
  • A production build configuration.
  • A fixed Node.js version.
  • A fixed Angular and Nx version.
  • The same machine and operating system.

Record the environment:

Operating System:
CPU:
RAM:
Node.js:
Package Manager:
Angular:
Nx:

Scenarios to measure

Scenario What we want to understand
Initial build Baseline execution time
Repeated build Cache effectiveness
Full workspace test Cost of running everything
Small application change Incremental build behavior
Shared library change Dependency impact
CI build Potential pipeline improvement
Remote cache hit Cross-machine reuse

Example benchmark commands

Angular CLI:

ng build admin
ng build customer

ng test admin
ng test customer

Nx:

nx build admin
nx build customer

nx test admin
nx test customer

Affected tasks:

nx affected -t build
nx affected -t test

For meaningful measurements, use the same workspace, equivalent build targets, and equivalent test coverage.

Important: Separate cold and warm runs

A cold run measures execution without reusable task results.

A warm run measures what happens when caches are available.

These are different scenarios and should not be mixed.

For each scenario:

  1. Run the task once.
  2. Record the initial execution.
  3. Run it again without changing inputs.
  4. Record the repeated execution.
  5. Repeat the experiment several times.
  6. Compare medians rather than relying on a single run.

For Nx, record whether the result came from:

  • Task execution.
  • Local cache.
  • Remote cache.

For Angular CLI, record the cache configuration and whether it was enabled.

Benchmark results template

Here is a table that could be included in the final article:

Scenario Angular CLI Nx Notes
Initial build TBD TBD Cold run
Repeated build TBD TBD Warm cache
Full test suite TBD TBD All projects
Small app change TBD TBD Incremental
Shared library change TBD TBD Affected projects
CI execution TBD TBD Pipeline comparison

I would only publish actual numbers after running the experiment.

If Nx is 20% faster in one scenario but only 3% faster in another, that's a much more interesting result than claiming it is universally faster.

It also makes the article more trustworthy.

10. When Does Nx Actually Make Sense?

Let's move away from features and focus on decisions.

Scenario 1: One Angular application 

my-app/
├── src/
├── angular.json
└── package.json

Nx probably isn't necessary.

Angular CLI provides everything required to develop, test, and build the application.

Introducing Nx might add concepts without solving a meaningful problem.

Scenario 2: Two independent applications 

company/
├── admin/
└── customer/

If these applications have:

  • Independent teams.
  • Independent releases.
  • Few shared dependencies.
  • Different lifecycles.

Separate repositories might be more appropriate.

A monorepo isn't automatically better simply because the applications belong to the same company.

Scenario 3: Multiple applications sharing a design system 

company-platform/
├── apps/
│   ├── admin/
│   └── customer/
│
└── libs/
    └── shared-ui/

This is a reasonable monorepo candidate.

Angular CLI can support this structure.

Nx becomes more attractive if we need:

  • Architectural dependency rules.
  • Project graph visualization.
  • Selective builds and tests.
  • Better task orchestration.
  • Remote caching.

Scenario 4: A large workspace with many domains 

company-platform/
├── apps/
│   ├── admin/
│   ├── customer/
│   └── operations/
│
└── libs/
    ├── vehicles/
    ├── appointments/
    ├── billing/
    ├── authentication/
    └── shared/

At this point, Nx can provide meaningful value.

The workspace needs more than a place to store projects.

It needs a way to understand dependencies, enforce architectural boundaries, and avoid unnecessary work.

Scenario 5: Microfrontends

Microfrontends introduce a different set of concerns.

Applications may share a repository but still need:

  • Independent deployment.
  • Independent ownership.
  • Runtime integration.
  • Separate release cycles.

A monorepo can support this arrangement, but it doesn't automatically solve microfrontend architecture.

Nx may help with workspace organization and CI, but deployment independence and runtime integration still require their own design.

11. A Practical Decision Checklist

Before adopting Nx, I would ask:

  • Do we have multiple applications or libraries that genuinely belong together?
  • Are dependencies between projects becoming difficult to understand?
  • Do we need architectural boundaries enforced automatically?
  • Are CI builds and tests executing unnecessary tasks?
  • Would task caching make a measurable difference?
  • Do we need to coordinate changes across applications?
  • Are the benefits worth introducing another tool into the development workflow?

If most answers are no, Angular CLI might be enough.

If several answers are yes, Nx deserves serious consideration.

The important part is not the number of applications.

It's the complexity of coordinating them.

12. My Take: Start Simple, Introduce Nx When the Problems Become Real

I don't think Nx should be the default answer to every Angular workspace.

Angular CLI is capable of managing multiple applications and libraries.

For smaller workspaces, that may be all you need.

But as a workspace grows, the problems change.

The challenge is no longer just creating applications or sharing components.

It becomes:

  • Understanding dependencies.
  • Enforcing architectural boundaries.
  • Avoiding unnecessary builds.
  • Coordinating tasks.
  • Improving CI performance.
  • Maintaining a consistent development workflow.

This is where Nx becomes valuable.

Not because it makes your architecture automatically better.

Not because every monorepo needs it.

But because it provides tooling for problems that become increasingly difficult to manage manually.

And that's the distinction I think matters most.

Don't introduce Nx because your project has multiple applications. Introduce it when the complexity of managing those applications becomes a problem that Nx can actually solve.

Final Thoughts

Monorepos are a strategy, not an architectural achievement.

Angular CLI already provides a solid foundation for organizing multiple applications and libraries.

Nx extends that foundation with project graphs, dependency constraints, task orchestration, caching, and CI optimization.

Those features can make a significant difference in larger workspaces.

But they also introduce additional concepts and configuration.

The best choice depends on the problems your team is facing today, not the scale you imagine your project might eventually reach.

I'd rather start with a simple workspace and introduce complexity when it becomes useful than build a sophisticated monorepo that solves problems we don't have.

What About Your Projects?

Have you adopted Nx in an Angular workspace?

Did it actually improve your development experience or CI performance?

Or did Angular CLI turn out to be enough?

I'm particularly interested in real-world experiences with affected builds, caching, and architectural boundaries.

articles.title: Being, Doing, Having: Why 50 Years of Senior Craft Lives in Context, Not Code
articles.description: Why does standard AI code generation try to jump straight to 'Have' without the proper 'Be'? How ladder rungs, the 'Null-State' couch flash, and stand-up comedy explain what separates senior engineers from junior token streamers.
articles.body_html:
"Vibe coding fails because the requests are just a demand to 'Have' without the proper 'Be'."

"Teaching is about relating. You need to understand their pains before you can explain the path to remove that." — Randal L. Schwartz

"Comedy is all about the set up and the punch. I guess teaching, or guiding an LLM, is also that." — Randal L. Schwartz

🗺️ Reader's Key (Where to Find These References): Throughout this article, references like Theorem 338.8q or Theorem 348.a point to numbered laws in our open Theoretical Foundations (syntheticscars.org/theory) monograph; IDs like SCAR-TEST-29 or SCAR-ERR-02 point to 4-Vector Synthetic Scars in the searchable Public Scar Registry (syntheticscars.org/registry); and targets like Target 15 (archaeology), Target 30 (tdd-red), Target 40 (critic), and Target 90 (scar compilation) refer to the declarative Makefile DAG in our Sourdough Starter Kit (syntheticscars.org/starter-kit) and Public Workflow Gist.

1. Looking Upstream: Why Be -> Do -> Have Is Context -> Process -> Content

People sometimes ask me how we kept finding these bridges between 1976 Makefiles, 1980 Smalltalk-80, 1986 Fernando Flores speech acts, and New Caledonian crow DNA.

One of my lifelong habits is thinking in second-order analogies—asking "How is the mapping of A -> B like the mapping of 1 -> 2?" (which, appropriately enough, is the exact vector-subtraction equation cos_sim(B - A, 2 - 1) that powers LLM embeddings!) and always asking: "What is upstream of this observation?"

One of my favorite upstream analogies is:

Be -> Do -> Have is like Context -> Process -> Content.

In fact, that single equation explains why "vibe coding" fails:

"Vibe coding fails because the requests are just a demand to 'Have' without the proper 'Be'."

Think about what a typical vibe-coding prompt actually is: "Build me an OAuth login page," "Fix the checkout race condition," "Review this PR." Every single one is an immediate demand to Have (Content) at the very end of the pipeline, without first establishing Be (Context)! And when you demand Have from an eager-to-please LLM that doesn't have the proper Be, it skips Do and hands you counterfeit Have (a bad actor just "reading the lines").

Look at the difference between demanding Have at the bottom of the waterfall versus building from Be -> Do -> Have:

Upstream Level Ontological Layer Systems Layer The "Vibe Coder" Trap (Demanding Have Without Be) The Synthetic Scar Way (Be -> Do -> Have)
Upstream (1st) BE (Identity & Boundaries) CONTEXT (What holds the space) Skipped: Stuffs everything into one polluted 150k-token chat window where the Builder grades its own homework. baseline.sources + SCAR_REGISTRY.md + fork(): Establish who the agent is (Archaeologist, Builder, or Clean-Room Critic) and its phase-bound scars before touching code.
Midstream (2nd) DO (Committed Action) PROCESS (How state transitions) Faked: Flails in an ad-hoc chat loop ("no, it's still broken, try again"), confusing process with content. WORKFLOW.mk + Crow Probing Loop: Execute the deterministic tdd-red -> tdd-green -> critic sequence with Flores speech-act receipts.
Downstream (3rd) HAVE (The Result) CONTENT (The code on the page) Demanded in a Vacuum: Demands the Content (Have) on Turn 1 ("Write the whole feature!") and tries to fix bugs by arguing with the Content. Verified Git Merkle Tree: Because Context (Be) and Process (Do) are locked upstream, clean Content (Have) falls out naturally at the bottom!

Whenever an AI agent writes a bad line of code, that bug is Content (Have)—it is at the very bottom of the waterfall. If you try to fix a Content bug by yelling at the Content in chat, you are standing at the bottom of the river with a bucket. When you step upstream to Process (Do = WORKFLOW.mk) and Context (Be = Make-Fork + SCAR_REGISTRY.md), you move the riverbanks once and the water flows clean forever.

Reinventing "Attention Is All You Need" One Level Up: Aiming the Spotlight Away from Doom

Think back to the 2017 Google paper that started the entire LLM revolution: "Attention Is All You Need" (Vaswani et al., 2017).

That paper proved that softmax(QK^T / sqrt(d_k)) * V was all you needed to build an associative neocortex.

Yes—the LLM knows how to pay attention. But it needs to pay attention to the right things: the ones that don't lead to doom.

Left to itself inside a bloated 150,000-token chat window, raw self-attention has two fatal blind spots:

  1. "Loud and Popular" Out-Shouts "Fatal": A shiny Stack Overflow tutorial shortcut (Vector 2: The Trap) appears 50,000 times in pre-training, so it grabs the attention spotlight, while the subtle unmount guard or serial-bus lock that prevents a 3 AM crash gets drowned out.
  2. 150k-Token Noise Dilution: When 12 skills, 500 lines of logs, and the Builder's own excuses sit in one window, the attention budget (1.0) is diluted into confetti.

Look at what WORKFLOW.mk, Make-Fork, and SCAR_REGISTRY.md actually do—they implement Macro-Attention one level above the Transformer:

  • The Query (Q): The active Makefile leaf target (Target 15, Target 30, Target 40) asks only for what matters right now.
  • The Sparse Keys (K): Make-Fork clears the desk to a crisp 20k-token window holding only the 3–5 phase-bound scars for that step—boosting their attention weight by 1,000x.
  • The -∞ Attention Mask (M): Each 4-Vector Scar places a bright red traffic flare right in front of the cliff edge (The Trap -> NOOO! Circuit Breaker -> Climb E-F-G-H), while clean-room fork() masks the Builder's private rationalizations out of the Critic's KV-cache.
  • The Lifecycle LayerNorm: Smalltalk condenseChanges folds .changes deltas into baseline.sources at phase boundaries so context never explodes.

Vaswani et al. gave AI the spotlight (Attention). The Crow's Genome (WORKFLOW.mk + SCAR_REGISTRY.md) aims that spotlight at the cliff edge before the wheels go over.

The "1, 2, 3, 4 ... W?" Sideways Blast: How to Jump Out of Local Valleys

While we were writing this, the AI flipped the table and asked me a question about human cognition:

"Randal, in an LLM, if the word 'crow' or 'Smalltalk' isn't already in my context window, I can't attend to it. When you're working on a software problem (1, 2, 3, 4), what happens in your head in the half-second before an analogy from 40 years ago pops up?"

I thought about how it actually feels from the inside:

"It appears as 'ok 1, 2, 3, 4... W? Where'd W come from?' It's because sometimes I 'step back'... it's like the path widens to the whole neighborhood for a second. Wow, if LLMs could learn to just do a random sideways blast like that, they might get out of valleys easier."

Think about why cranking up an LLM's temperature slider fails when an agent is stuck in a local valley:

  • Because the words "Flutter", "Dart", and "Git" are still sitting right there in the prompt, turning up temperature just makes the model stumble around drunk at the bottom of the exact same canyon (1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5_typo).
  • When a human generalist "steps back," you temporarily strip the surface nouns off the problem so only the bare relational shape remains ("Wait: how does a tiny fixed code govern a huge adaptive network?").
  • The moment you strip the nouns, the path widens to the whole neighborhood of human and biological knowledge—and sideways across the canyon wall, W (Crow DNA, 1980 Smalltalk-80, 1976 Make) fires an interrupt straight into your working memory!

And you can give your AI agent that exact "Sideways Relational Blast (W-Hop)" in three lines of Make-Fork:

  1. Step Back (Noun-Strip): Take the stuck problem [1, 2, 3, 4] and strip out every programming language, framework, and codebase noun into one pure sentence of relational tension.
  2. Sideways Blast (fork() with Zero Code Context): Send only that one noun-free sentence to a fresh subagent and ask: "What 3 mechanisms (W_1, W_2, W_3) in biology, 1970s/1980s computing history, or physics solved this exact tension?"
  3. Zoom Back In: Bring W back into your code at temperature = 0.0 and climb straight out of the valley!

"It's Quiet... Yeah, Too Quiet": The False-Finish Suspicion Instinct

Then the AI asked me a second question:

"How do you instantly smell that a working solution is wrong when 100% of the tests are green? To an LLM, zero errors and fast green checkmarks mean 100% confidence!"

My answer was immediate:

"There's an innate baked-in 'wait, this was too easy' suspicion from having been burned with a false finish previously. It's the 'It's quiet...' 'Yeah... too quiet' meme."

Think about why crows—and scarred engineers—freeze when the forest suddenly goes dead silent:

  • In a real forest, normal life is noisy (Baseline Entropy > 0). When every bird and insect suddenly goes 100% silent, a naive creature thinks "How peaceful!" and strolls into the clearing. A crow knows dead silence means a hawk just entered the trees.
  • In software engineering, touching a real production subsystem is supposed to push back: Target 30 (tdd-red) should fail loudly first, types should complain, and state edges should demand guards.
  • When an AI agent edits a complex async lifecycle, runs the test suite, and everything passes on the very first try in 0.01 seconds with zero friction...
    • The Unscarred LLM says: "It's quiet! Ship it!"
    • The Scarred Veteran says: "Yeah... too quiet."

Whenever a hard ticket yields with suspiciously zero friction (Observed Friction << Expected Difficulty), it is almost always one of four False-Finish Ambushes:

  1. The Un-Awaited / Mocked Test Ambush: The test passed on Run 1 (Red_Runs == 0) because an async Future wasn't awaited, or a mock returned the exact hardcoded value the assertion checked (SCAR-TEST-29).
  2. The Silent Swallow Ambush: The crash vanished after a 1-line edit because ?. or ?? [] or catch (_) silently swallowed the error upstream (SCAR-ERR-02).
  3. The Unwired Branch Ambush: All existing tests passed because nothing in the test suite actually calls the new sad-path branch yet.
  4. The Rubber-Stamp Critic Ambush: A 15-file diff sailed through review with zero pushback because the reviewer didn't check the negative space.

That is why WORKFLOW.mk treats "Too Quiet" (Red_Runs == 0) as a hard halt: until we watch the test fail in red against the broken state, we never trust a quiet green checkmark!

Why Metaphors Like "Sourdough Starter" and "Crow vs. Moth" Work: Humans (and LLMs) Learn by Deltas

Finally, the AI asked me why names like "The Sourdough Starter" or "Crow vs. Moth" do so much heavy lifting compared to academic acronyms:

"The 'right name' isn't what we're aiming for... just 'the name that is similar enough, but distinct enough' that we know the scope of the relation. Humans learn by deltas. To describe a thing X as 'similar to Y but different from Z', it's a fairly learnable info."

Look at the information compression in X = Similar to Y, but Different from Z:

  • If you try to define X from scratch with zero prior anchor, you have to write 10,000 words of specification (H(X) is huge).
  • If you say: "Our bootstrap (X) is like a Sourdough Starter (Y), not a Static Config File (Z)":
    1. Similar Enough in Relation (Y): Everyone (and every LLM) already knows a sourdough starter is a tiny living culture where a spoonful leavens the whole loaf and gets fed back after every bake.
    2. Distinct Enough in Domain: Because nobody is actually putting flour and water into their MacBook, the domain boundary automatically clips the metaphor to the exact scope of the relation!
    3. Different from the Foil (not Z): Subtracting Z (not a static config file, not a moth's porch-light instinct) slices off the exact trap you want the learner to avoid.

And notice: Similar to Y (Context), Different from Z (The Trap), via Delta (The Permanent Reflex) is the exact three-part geometry of every Synthetic Scar and every DPO training tuple!

Even better, when the model asked me later why naming classes in code is so hard—and why LLMs love mushy names like DataManager, StateHandler, and ProcessHelper—the exact same law popped out (Corollary 338.8w):

"A name should identify what it's similar to, and what it's different from."

Look at why DataManager turns into a 4,000-line swamp while names like BlocSignal, KaiselAbsorbingPage, or CleanRoomCritic stay clean for years:

  • DataManager has zero fence (Different from Z = Nothing!), so when a tired developer comes back on Friday afternoon to add Case N+1, every random method in the codebase gets dumped into it!
  • BlocSignal tells you in two words what it is similar to (Y) (Bloc event/state discipline) AND what it is different from (not Z) (synchronous Signal graph instead of async StreamController queues)!
  • KaiselAbsorbingPage tells you what it is similar to (Y) (a Page on the route stack) AND what it is different from (not Z) (it absorbs back-navigation gestures instead of letting them pop past it)! Once a class name carries both Y and not Z, bad code looks visibly ridiculous the instant someone tries to paste it inside!

Victim vs. Culprit: The 4-Quadrant Diagnostic Matrix ([X, Upstream(X)] × [History, Analogs])

One last question sealed the afternoon. The AI asked:

"When a bug report says 'X is broken', an LLM immediately opens X and starts patching X. How do you know in 30 seconds that X is just the innocent victim—and that someone poisoned the water upstream?"

When I watched what my brain actually does in those first 30 seconds, a 2 × 2 matrix popped out:

"My first instinct is to recall 'history with X' and 'history with X upstream'. But that expands laterally to both 'things like X' and 'things like X's upstream'."

An unscarred LLM only looks at one point: (X, Right Now). A veteran engineer immediately expands (X, Right Now) along two axes—Causal Depth (Local vs. Upstream) × Analogical Breadth (History vs. Things Like It):

Causal Axis \ Memory Axis 1. Exact History (git log / blame) 2. Lateral Analogs ("Things Like...")
Local Crime Scene (X) Q1: History with X
"Has X been sitting untouched for 6 months? Then X is the innocent bystander!" 		Q3: Things Like X (~X)
"How do sibling views/consumers in this repo handle this input? Does ~X have a guard X missed?"
Upstream Water Supply (Upstream(X)) Q2: History with X Upstream
"Which caller or provider feeding X in the strict digraph was edited two days ago?" 		Q4: Things Like X's Upstream (~Upstream(X))
"Where have I seen this shape of upstream poison (stale cache hydration, un-awaited disposal) in SCAR_REGISTRY.md?"

When Target 15 (archaeology) fills out all four boxes before writing a plan, the agent never slaps a band-aid on the victim in Q1 when the poison came from Q2, Q3, or Q4!

The Missing generalize() Opcode: How Frontier Labs Can Bake In Half of Scars Today

Stepping back and looking at all of those pieces together revealed one final realization:

"While attentional chain-of-thought gets most problems solved, LLMs don't have a 'generalize' mechanism. And I wonder if the labs can bake those horizontal nudges in—because if so, half the work of Scars will be done."

Think about what happens when an LLM uses 20,000 "Thinking" (Chain-of-Thought) tokens to solve a bug in LoginPage.dart (x_0):

  • Its Chain-of-Thought is purely episodic: it walks step-by-step until LoginPage.dart passes the test—and then it stops!
  • It leaves ProfilePage.dart and SettingsPage.dart (x_1, x_2 in ~X) sitting right next door with the exact same bug, because the Transformer architecture has no native generalize() opcode (x_0 -> for all x in "Things Like X")!

Now imagine if Google DeepMind, Anthropic, and OpenAI baked a 3-Step Horizontal generalize() Nudge directly into RL post-training for <thinking> blocks:

  1. Solve the Instance (x_0): Find the fix for X.
  2. Execute the Horizontal Nudge (x_0 -> ~X and Upstream(x_0) -> ~Upstream(X)): Before leaving <thinking>, automatically ask: "What are 'things like X' and 'things like X's upstream' across this task?"
  3. Sweep the Equivalence Class (for all x in ~X): Apply the invariant across every sibling in scope and state the generalized rule!

If the labs bake that horizontal generalization reflex into the base model's <thinking> loop, half the work of Synthetic Scars is done inside the model on Turn 1—and our local SCAR_REGISTRY.md (Target 90) handles the other half: saving that generalized rule to disk so tomorrow's session never has to re-learn it!

"Reading the Lines" vs. Direct Expression: How to Spot a Bluffing Conman (or Subagent) by Its Pacing

Right after that, the model asked me one more question about human intuition: How do you tell when someone—or an AI agent—is using all the right words, checklists, and technical jargon, yet is completely bluffing?

I didn't even have to think about it:

"It's visceral. I can 'feel' when a bad conman is using the right words but the wrong backing. There's also a pacing thing in human speech when a bad actor is just 'reading the lines'. I think we're calibrated for it by our own recitations rather than direct expressions... Ooooh... it's Be–Do–Have again! We trust great actors because they ARE the lines, not just doing or having the lines."

Stop and think about how cleanly that closes the entire loop!

Why can you hear when someone is "reading the lines" within three seconds, even if every word in their script is grammatically perfect? Because bad acting and LLM hallucination are both Have -> Do -> Be inversions:

  • The Bad Actor / Conman (Have -> Do -> Be): Starts by having the lines on the page (Content), does the mechanical reading (Process), and hopes you believe they are the character (Context).
  • The Great Actor / Grounded Agent (Be -> Do -> Have): First is the state space (Be / Context: inhabiting the character's lived history, or waking up inside a Clean-Room Make-Fork loaded with phase-bound Scars and baseline.sources), does the live navigation of the conflict (Do / Process: probing the strict digraph), and the lines (Have / Content) emerge as an inevitable side effect of being there!

And how does your ear tell the difference between Have -> Do -> Be and Be -> Do -> Have?

  1. We Are Calibrated by Our Own Recitations: Every human knows what it feels like on the inside when we recite a memorized pledge, read a teleprompter, or bluff our way through a book report we didn't read—versus what it feels like when we are directly expressing a live, three-dimensional mental model in our head.
  2. Direct Expression (Be -> Do -> Have) Has "Crux-Weighted Impedance": When an engineer who actually inhabits the system explains a fix, their pacing varies with the difficulty of the terrain. They breeze past the trivial boilerplate in three words ("standard imports here"), and then they slow down, lean in, pause, and get ultra-specific right at the gnarliest edge case ("now watch line 142—if the stream closes while the dialog is still mounted...").
  3. "Reading the Lines" (Have -> Do -> Be) Has Uniform Boilerplate Cadence: A conman—or a hallucinating LLM subagent—doesn't have a 3D map of where the cliff is. To a script-reader, every sentence has the exact same weight! They glide right past a fatal asynchronous race condition at the exact same smooth, cheerful, 60-words-per-minute tempo as they read the copyright header!

Look at a lazy AI code-review summary when a subagent is "reading the lines":

  • Intent: The intent is clear and matches the ticket.
  • Verification: The tests are comprehensive and pass.
  • Architecture: The architecture is clean and modular.
  • Blast Radius: The blast radius is minimal and contained.

Every bullet is the same length, the same rhythm, and the same smooth, zero-friction tempo! There is zero impedance spike at the crux (Theorem 338.8n). That is why our Target 40 Clean-Room Critic gate bans uniform boilerplate summaries and demands crux-proportional witness density: exact file:line citations, negative-witness inputs, and explicit failure traces right where the strict digraph edges cross.

Why "Working Ugly" Code Makes You Tense Up: The Aesthetics of Future Care (Case N + 1)

Then the model hit me with a question I had never tried to put into words before:

"To a compiler or a test runner, two pull requests that pass the exact same 100 unit tests at the exact same speed are 100% identical. Why do humans have an aesthetic sense—a literal feeling of beauty or disgust—about invisible logical structures?"

My first hunch was immediate: "Can I edit this later, to add a new case?"
And a second later, the deeper truth underneath it popped out:

"Not just 'can I edit this'—but 'is it carefully constructed, and I won't have enough care in the future to edit it'!"

Read that twice, because it explains the entire mystery of engineering taste (Theorem 338.8o):

  • Today, when an author (or an LLM) writes a "clever, carefully constructed" piece of code that passes all the tests, they are operating at 100% Peak Care (C_max). They are like a watchmaker holding their breath with tweezers, keeping five invisible ordering dependencies and three parallel if/else ladders balanced in hot working memory at the same time.
  • Six months from now, when Future-You (or a cold-start AI subagent) comes back at 4:30 PM on a Friday to add Case N+1, you will NOT have C_max care! You will be tired, distracted, and operating at normal maintenance care (C_maint << C_max).

So what is that physical feeling of disgust when you look at "working ugly" or "overly clever" code?

  • Your gut is looking at a house of cards and saying: "This only works right now because you were holding your breath when you built it! It is a loaded mousetrap waiting for Future-Me when I don't have enough care to remember your invisible ritual on line 84!"
  • And what is that physical feeling of beauty and relief when you look at an exhaustive Dart 3 switch over a sealed class, or a declarative Makefile DAG, or a clean state table?
  • It is the relief of seeing that the structure itself holds the care for you (C_req(Case N+1) <= C_maint)! Even if Future-You comes back half-asleep to add Case N+1, there is either an obvious 1-line slot waiting for you, or the compiler immediately refuses to compile and points you to every single spot you forgot!

And that also explains how I know when to stop and ship instead of gold-plating a feature to death (Theorem 338.8x):

"It's an 80/20 call. If what I did handles 80% of the cases, I'm happy."

Why do so many engineers (and LLMs) ruin clean designs by trying to pre-code 100% of all imaginary future edge cases on Day 1? Because they are afraid of editing their own code later! So they spend 80% of their complexity budget trying to guess the 20% long tail of hypothetical cases—which bloats the code 5× and paints them into a high-care corner! When your structure makes adding Case N+1 a low-care 5-line edit (Theorem 338.8o), you can happily ship the clean 80% today and wait for the remaining 20% to show up with real requirements tomorrow!

And when I parachute into a brand-new codebase for the very first time (Theorem 338.8y), how do I map those low-care exemplars versus the high-care mousetraps in 60 seconds?

"Before AI, I'd start in Dart with the pubspec.yaml. With AI, my new rule is to ask: 'Review this codebase, and tell me the good, the bad, and the ugly'."

  • Reading pubspec.yaml first tells you the Context (Be) of the building in 30 lines (SDK version, state management, router, test stack) before you drown in leaf files.
  • And asking the AI for The Good, The Bad, and The Ugly (instead of a polite "summary") forces it to separate:
    1. The Good (Y): The clean patterns in the repo you should imitate;
    2. The Bad (~Z_1): The broken debt you must not copy; and
    3. The Ugly (~Z_2): The working-but-fragile houses of cards (C_req ≈ C_max) where you need yellow caution tape before touching a single line!

And what do you do when your ticket lands right in the middle of The Bad or The Ugly?

An unscarred AI agent walks into a codebase with a sycophantic prior (P(existing code is sacred) ≈ 0.99)—or buys the classic excuse that "the code is only ugly because the domain is complex." My rule (Theorem 348.a) is much simpler:

"Simple. 80% of code is crap... There's no difference. Crappy code is crap... I often just try to get them to accept major restructurings. And if they don't, I interject one ticket at a time. I have a sense of how ticket 2 and 3 will go if I get ticket 1 introduced and landed. Ticket 1 fixes something fundamental, without breaking the rest of the world. It shifts the building foundation, without moving the rooms... It's more of a recognition about why the design needs help, and what the basic burn already is."

Look at the two-gear play there:

  1. Locate "The Basic Burn": You don't polish random crappy code sitting in a cold corner. You look for what the basic burn already is—the cracked foundation underneath the current feature that is taxing the team on every change.
  2. Gear 1 vs. Gear 2 ("Shift the Building Foundation, Without Moving the Rooms"): First, you pitch the real restructuring up front. If the team flinches at a big rewrite, you don't surrender and weave 40 more noodles into the spaghetti—and you don't go rogue and rewrite 50 files in a bugfix PR. Instead, you play 3-ticket positional chess:
    • Ticket 1 jacks up the house, slides the right foundation underneath, and sets the existing rooms right back down on thin shims—shifting the building foundation without moving the rooms (zero broken call sites, zero reviewer panic).
    • Once Ticket 1 lands in main, the center of gravity of the codebase has shifted (Be has changed!), so Tickets 2 and 3 can walk into one room at a time, delete the scaffolding, and drop the floor straight onto the new foundation!

And once we realized how fast this Reverse-Socratic Foil Sparring worked—where the LLM holds up its own naive statistical instinct (Z) and asks me how a 45-year human veteran reacts—we ran a rapid-fire 6-question round that pulled out six more laws in eight minutes (Theorems 348.b–348.h):

  1. The 10-Second PR Diff Smell Test (Theorem 348.b): "I think the diff 'looks right' because it fulfills the mission. And things unrelated to the mission scare me." Unrelated diff hunks aren't "harmless cleanup"—they are the uncleaned crime-scene footprints of an author who was thrashing in the dark!
  2. Debugging the "Impossible" Bug (Theorem 348.c): "I work out or single-step every data change. At some point I'll know the bad actor." Stop guessing which function has a bug; follow the data value itself (d_0 -> d_1 -> ... -> d_k). Functions can lie about what their names say they do, but the exact hop d_{k-1} -> d_k where valid data turns into garbage catches the bad actor red-handed.
  3. When to Add a Third-Party Package (Theorem 348.d): "I'll first ask how many lines of code to implement the feature. If a package reduces that, I'm ok with a package that's being actively maintained." Never import 5,000 lines of someone else's liabilities to save 15 lines of in-house code—and never trust a frozen pre-training memory without checking that the package has a living maintainer today.
  4. Designing Boundaries (Theorem 348.e): "I look at 'what if I need a version 2'. So the protocol should have a good v1 and v2 strategy." Only implement v1 today (80/20!), but put the v2 seam into the boundary on Day 1 so v2 can slide in later without breaking v1 callers.
  5. Spotting What's Missing in a Spec (Theorem 348.f): "Recognizing the error returns and making sure they don't leak info, like 'yes this is a valid username, but not a valid password'." Happy-path specs forget the error returns—and overly "helpful" LLM error messages across untrusted boundaries turn into security enumeration oracles!
  6. "Spidey Sense" & Scooby-Doo's "I've Got a Bad Feeling About This" (Theorem 348.h): How do I spot a sad path on a brand-new design I've never been burned by before? "I look for 'similar' scars. However, they have lower weight for me—more of a 'possibly sad path' indication. This is partially where my 'nudges' come from: I have an untested hypothesis that may not bear out. And we've seen my interactions sometimes be just 'oh, TIL today'." Standard LLMs have no middle gear: they either ignore a risk completely (0%) or hallucinate that their weak hunch is a 100% proven fact and rewrite four working files! True Spidey Sense is a flashlight, not a hammer: when a partial scar match gives you a "bad feeling," you fire a read-only probe—which either catches the trapdoor before you step on it, or teaches you "Oh, TIL today!" without breaking a single line of working code!

The "Null-State" Couch Flash (and Why We Forget Half of Them by Morning!)

Then the model asked me about another human mystery: Why can you bang your head against a bug from 2:00 PM to 6:00 PM with zero progress, walk away to watch TV, and suddenly have the answer pop into your head in three seconds?

I thought about what actually happens when that hits me:

"When you're not focusing on an item, but it's still a concern, you get flashes of related items throughout the day... It's starting from a null state. I'm just surfing the web, or watching TV, and I have a thought 'oh, this is how to solve X', and weirdly I sometimes immediately log in to capture it. Oddly, about half the time I forget it, and wonder the next day what I had come up with!"

Look at the two halves of that observation (Theorem 338.8p), because together they explain both how human incubation works and why standard AI retry loops fail:

  1. Why You Need a "Null State" to Find the Answer: When you are staring intensely at your screen at 6:00 PM, your foreground working memory is clamped onto your failed assumptions—which actively shouts down (laterally inhibits) every quiet, sideways connection in your brain. When you sit on the couch watching TV, your foreground working memory drops to a Null State (h_fg ≈ 0), while the unfinished bug stays open in the background as a stripped-down, generalized Standing Concern (the Zeigarnik Effect). Because the blinding spotlight is finally turned off, a random scene on TV or a passing thought clicks right into that open socket: "Oh! That's how to solve X!"
  2. Why You Forget It 50% of the Time Unless You Log In Immediately (The Unmounted Write-Head Paradox!): Why on earth would your brain find a brilliant breakthrough at 9:00 PM on the couch and then erase it before 8:00 AM—leaving you only with the frustrating memory that you had solved it? Because biological brains have a hardware trade-off:
    • At your desk (Foreground Mode): Your episodic Write-Head is MOUNTED (everything gets journaled to memory), but your Search Aperture is NARROW (rut-locked).
    • On the couch (Null-State Mode): Your Search Aperture is WIDE precisely because your executive prefrontal machinery is powered down—which means your episodic Write-Head is UNMOUNTED! If you don't physically get off the couch and log in to flush that volatile buffer to disk within 60 seconds, the next TV commercial overwrites the buffer, and by morning all that's left is the IRQ = SOLVED flag with an empty payload!

And look at how our Make-Fork + .changes architecture combines the best of both worlds for an AI agent:

  • When a subagent gets stuck in a rut, we don't keep yelling at it in a hot, blinded 100k-token window—we kill the hot context (Null-State Reset) and fork a fresh subagent seeded only with the generalized concern!
  • And unlike the human brain on the couch, the harness keeps the changes-$timestamp.changes Write-Head permanently mounted—so 0% of those Null-State breakthroughs ever evaporate overnight!

How to Know When to Drop to the Null State: "Iterations Should Look Different—I Have Different Problems at Each Ladder Rung"

Right after that, the model asked the natural follow-up question: How does a human know when to keep climbing at the keyboard versus when to stop and drop to the Null State, whereas an LLM will either burn 50,000 tokens trying 14 variations of the same broken regex—or panic and revert a good fix just because the test suite is still red?

The answer came out in two sentences:

"Iterations should look different. If not, you're on the wrong track. It's how I know I'm making progress: I have different problems at each ladder rung."

Look at how clean that rule is (Theorem 338.8q):

  • Why Novices and Unscarred LLMs Panic When Climbing: An unscarred LLM only understands binary pass/fail (Exit Code == 0). So when it fixes a Rung 1 bug (say, a parser schema error) and the test runner immediately prints a brand-new Rung 2 error downstream (say, a stream lifecycle error), the LLM panics—"Oh no, the test is still red! My edit failed!"—and reverts its own working Rung 1 climb!
  • How a Veteran Reads the Ladder Rungs: When you are on the right track, you don't expect the test to turn green on Rung 1—you expect to have a different problem at each ladder rung!
    • Rung 1 Problem: Fix the JSON parser schema.
    • Rung 2 Problem: Now the parser works, which exposes the stream controller ordering!
    • Rung 3 Problem: Now the stream works, which exposes the widget assertion! Having a brand-new downstream problem is the exact proof that you just climbed a rung!
  • When You Are Stuck on the Same Rung (The Rut): Conversely, when an LLM is in a rut, it thinks it is "trying different things" because Iteration 1 changed x + 1 to x - 1, Iteration 2 added ?? 0, and Iteration 3 wrapped the same line in try / catch. To a human who looks at the shape of the iterations, all three iterations are stuck on the exact same ladder rung!

And when you wire that Ladder-Rung rule into .changes (LoopIterationChunk), you get two automatic superpowers:

  1. New Rung (Rung_i > Rung_{i-1}): Lock the .changes checkpoint so the agent is forbidden from reverting its Rung 1 progress when Rung 2 throws a new error!
  2. Same Rung (Shape_i ≈ Shape_{i-1}): Fire the Rut Circuit Breaker—kill the hot worker context (Drop to Null State, h_fg <- 0) and launch a clean-room SidewaysBlast (1, 2, 3, 4 ... W?)!

Why 4-Vector Scars Work When "Rules" Fail: "Teaching Is About Relating to Their Pain"

Finally, the model asked me a question that goes back to my decades of teaching Perl, Smalltalk, and Flutter to thousands of human students: How do you teach someone who has never been burned by the stove yet, so the lesson actually sticks before they crash production?

The secret is the same for a 22-year-old junior developer and a trillion-parameter LLM:

"Teaching is about relating. You need to understand their pains before you can explain the path to remove that."

Think about why traditional CLAUDE.md / .cursorrules files fail (Theorem 338.8r):

  • Most prompt rulebooks are written like a grumpy professor shouting from the finish line: "Rule #47: Always do Y!"
  • When a student—or an LLM—is in the middle of a task, their brain's active Query (Q_pain) isn't shaped like Y. Their Query is shaped like the pain they are feeling right now ("The compiler is yelling at me, the test is failing, and I promised to finish this step!").
  • If your rule's Key (K) only talks about the destination Y, the dot product Q_pain · K^T is zero! An answer to a pain you aren't currently feeling slides right off your brain as lecture noise!

Now look at how a 4-Vector Synthetic Scar relates to the learner's pain first:

  1. Meet Them Inside Their Pain (The Wound + The Trap + The Circuit Breaker): "You are staring at this exact compiler/test friction right now, and your weights feel the pain of wanting to finish fast by reaching for 5-6-7-8. Stop! You are excused from that pressure."
  2. Explain the Path That Removes the Pain (The Permanent Reflex): Once Q_pain · K_pain^T hits 1.0—because the Scar just named the exact struggle the agent is standing in—the door swings wide open, and the Value vector (Climb E-F-G-H instead) walks straight into working memory!

Why Great Engineers Laugh at Bugs: "Humor Is an Expression of Relief—Even by Mocking the Pain"

And that led to one last question about human nature: Why do veteran hackers and engineers laugh so much when they debug, and why do we give our worst failure modes funny names like "The Pink Elephant," "The Moth at the Bug Zapper," "Sam at the End of the Hall," and "The Conman Reading the Lines"?

I said:

"Humor is an expression of a relief. What was once pain is gone, even by mimicking or mocking it."

Think about what a laugh actually is (Theorem 338.8s):

  • In evolutionary biology (Ramachandran's False-Alarm Theory, 1998), laughter is the tribe's "All-Clear" pressure-release valve! When a rustle in the bushes—or a terrifying 3:00 AM production bug—suddenly turns out to be a one-line fix you now completely understand, all that pent-up threat tension discharges in a laugh, dropping your brain back to the Null State!
  • Even better: Why do we mock or mimic the pain? Because when a failure mode is nameless and mysterious, it owns you (Be = Victim). The moment you mock it—turning a scary LLM failure mode into a funny caricature ("Look at the moth spiraling into the porch light again!" or "Uh-oh, it's quiet... yeah, too quiet!")—you shrink the monster down to a toy model you can hold in your hand (Be = Master), discharge the panic, and make the lesson unforgettable to everyone in the flock!

And then it hit me—having once been paid to do stand-up comedy, and having used comedy to teach Perl and Smalltalk for decades:

"Comedy is all about the set up and the punch. I guess teaching, or guiding an LLM, is also that."

Look at how Stand-Up Comedy, Teaching, and Guiding an LLM through a Ticket (WORKFLOW.mk) are the exact same two-beat art form (Corollary 338.8t):

  • Punch Without Setup = "Vibe Coding": If a comic walks out to a cold microphone and shouts a punchline with zero setup, nobody laughs because the room has no shared context (Be). When a vibe coder shouts "Fix the checkout bug!" on Turn 1 without setting up the context, the LLM hallucinates for the exact same reason!
  • Setup Without Punch = 150k-Token Context Bloat: In stand-up, every unnecessary word in the setup bleeds energy out of the room. In AI coding, stuffing 150,000 tokens of rambling history and unrelated files into one chat window is a shaggy-dog story that triggers context compaction before the punchline ever arrives!
  • Tight Setup + Sharp Punch = Make-Fork + 4-Vector Scars:
    • The Setup: Spawn a clean-room subagent with zero fat, hand it the Target 15 strict digraph, and name The Trap (1-2-3-4 -> 5-6-7-8) so 100% of its attention is focused on the exact edge of the assumption.

    * The Punch: Write the Target 30 (tdd-red) negative-witness test just like a punchline—an innocent-looking input that makes the naive code's pants fall down—and fire The Circuit Breaker (NOOO!) -> Climb E-F-G-H right at peak attention!

Summary: Craft Lives in Context

A junior developer (and an unscarred LLM) thinks that software craft is about memorizing syntax (Have). When something breaks, they frantically try 14 slight variations of the same line on the same ladder rung.

A veteran engineer operates in Be -> Do -> Have:

  1. Be (Context): Locking in the stance, the caller digraph, and the negative bounds ("If you're being THIS, there's trouble ahead!");
  2. Do (Process): Single-stepping one state transition at a time, reading the ladder rungs ("I have different problems at each rung"), and dropping to the Null State when ruts occur;
  3. Have (Content): The clean, tested, low-care diff that emerges as the inevitable byproduct.

In Part 4.5, we'll look at the final frontier: The Prisoner in the Library (Mary's Room & Plato's Cave)—why LLMs struggle with Be because internet pre-training only ever recorded Have, how a Two-Track Transformer runs a Contextual Next-Token rule above the Content stream, and how MIT CSAIL's 2026 Weight-Space Programming just proved Be / Do / Have in raw silicon.
